strengths: The core method (SANTA) is clearly motivated and cleanly formulated: sampling S value rows from the post-softmax distribution gives an unbiased estimator of the value aggregation with a controllable 1/S variance knob, and the variance-reduced S^2ANTA variants (stratified/systematic) are a natural and well-executed extension.

The theoretical analysis, while not deep, is correct and complete for what is claimed: unbiasedness, 1/S variance scaling, a stratified variance-dominance theorem (Theorem A.6), and a vector Bernstein tail; empirical variance measurements (Appendix D) match the theoretical slopes.

Systems contribution is real: the paper identifies the actual GPU parallelization challenge (sampling requires a global CDF, breaking the split-KV associativity used by FlashDecoding) and proposes two concrete kernel designs (proportional budget allocation with a global sync vs. speculative per-tile sampling with deferred normalization), with full pseudocode.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: GSM8K, MMLU, and RULER-style long-context tasks across Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, and BitNet-2B; comparisons against both FlashInfer/FlashDecoding (kernel latency) and top-k attention (accuracy); bootstrap confidence intervals throughout.

The paper is notably honest about limitations: it explicitly shows prefill gains do NOT translate to sparse memory access (Table 9, >94% V rows read), acknowledges kernel-level (not end-to-end) speedups and Amdahl's Law, and correctly frames Bernoulli qKT sampling as preliminary/complementary rather than a headline result.

Detailed reproducibility material: microbenchmark protocol (Appendix Q) documents cold-cache thrashing, timing methodology, and an asymmetry in FlashDecoding's fused append; prompting/grading protocols are fully specified (Appendix N); licenses are listed.
weaknesses: The headline speedup (1.5x) is kernel-level only, at batch size 1, on a single consumer-class GPU (RTX 6000 Ada), with no end-to-end generation latency or throughput measurements. Since decode attention is only a fraction of end-to-end decode time, the practical benefit at the system level is unquantified; the paper acknowledges Amdahl's Law but does not measure it.

The fundamental coverage is limited: the score stage still requires reading the full key cache, so only roughly half of the KV bandwidth is addressable. A 1.5x reduction in a component that itself is only part of decode time yields modest real-world gains, and the paper does not report them.

Novelty is moderate. Monte Carlo/sampling-based attention approximation exists (Kim & Ko 2022 is cited), stratified and systematic sampling are textbook techniques (Cochran, Lohr, Owen are cited as such), and top-k candidate selection is a well-studied deterministic alternative. The contribution is primarily a careful systems realization plus empirical characterization rather than a new algorithmic idea.

The accuracy-matching operating points raise questions about sensitivity: S^2ANTA-flash needs S=2048 (16x the budget of prop) to match accuracy, revealing high variance of the speculative scheme; and the choice of 'smallest S matching accuracy' is a form of selection on the test tasks (4 RULER tasks at a single 32k context length) without held-out tuning.

Some evaluation regimes weaken the central bandwidth claim: the GSM8K/MMLU analyses use contexts of only ~341-424 tokens, where S << nk barely holds and savings are marginal; the strongest evidence is concentrated in the 32k RULER subset with modest task diversity.

The open-source release statement is incomplete ('We open-source our kernels at:' followed by nothing), which undercuts the reproducibility claim for the most implementation-heavy part of the work (custom CUDA kernels).

The Bernoulli qKT component is underdeveloped relative to its billing: it achieves only ~15% key-access reduction under GQA (85% of features still fetched), tolerates a 30% score error only in the BitNet setting, and its end-to-end utility relative to simpler score-stage baselines (e.g., SparQ, cited) is not established.

Missing analysis of stochasticity effects on generation beyond aggregate accuracy: no study of output distribution shift, token-level divergence vs. SDPA, or sensitivity of long multi-turn generation to per-step estimator noise at aggressive budgets.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-executed: sampling S indices from the post-softmax distribution and aggregating only the corresponding value rows gives an unbiased estimator of the attention output while replacing value-stage multiply-accumulates with gather-and-add. The formal treatment is sound: unbiasedness (Prop. A.2), 1/S variance scaling (Prop. A.3), a Loewner-order variance-dominance theorem for stratified sampling (Thm. A.6), and a vector Bernstein tail (Thm. B.1) are all correctly stated and proved.

The systems contribution is real and non-trivial. The paper identifies a genuine GPU implementation obstacle — sampling creates a sequential dependency on the global CDF that conflicts with split-KV parallelism — and proposes two distinct solutions (global proportional budget allocation vs. speculative per-tile sampling with deferred normalization), with full pseudocode (Algs. 2–8).

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this kind of paper: two models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), three benchmark families (GSM8K, MMLU, RULER long-context tasks at 4k–32k tokens), bootstrap confidence intervals throughout, a comparison against deterministic top-k attention, a detailed and honest microbenchmark protocol (Appendix Q, including cold-cache L2 thrashing), empirical variance validation matching the theoretical 1/S slope, and ablations (layer sensitivity, per-layer budget allocation via REINFORCE).

Limitations are handled honestly: the paper explicitly acknowledges that prefill gains no sparse-memory benefit (Appendix F shows >94% of V rows are read even at S=16), that S²ANTA-flash requires a 16× larger budget (S=2048 vs. 128) to match accuracy, that reported speedups are kernel-level and subject to Amdahl's Law, and that multiplier-free arithmetic does not currently help on tensor-core GPUs. This honesty is a virtue and the claims that are made are generally supported.

The comparison to top-k attention (Tables 11–15) is meaningful: SANTA variants match or exceed top-k accuracy at equal budget while eliminating multiplications, and the multi-hop QA gains (~5% on QA2) are plausibly explained by the unbiasedness argument (information not concentrated in top-k keys).
weaknesses: No end-to-end speedup is reported. All latency claims are decode-step attention-kernel-only at batch size 1 on a single RTX 6000 Ada. The paper concedes Amdahl's Law applies, but never quantifies the end-to-end decode speedup or the effect at realistic serving batch sizes (>1), where kernel behavior and the memory-bound regime change substantially. The headline 1.5× figure therefore overstates practical impact without supporting end-to-end evidence.

Missing comparison against the closest prior methods at the systems level. MagicPIG (Chen et al., 2025) is a sampling-based LSH attention method published at ICLR 2025 that is directly relevant, and Quest (Tang et al., 2024) and SparQ (Ribar et al., 2024) are strong decoding-side sparse-attention baselines; they appear in the related-work discussion but are not included in the kernel-latency or accuracy comparisons (only top-k is compared). This weakens the claim that the kernel speedup is meaningfully attributable to the proposed design rather than to a general sparsity budget.

Per-layer unbiasedness does not imply the end-to-end model output is in any useful sense 'unbiased': each layer's stochastic output is fed through many subsequent non-linear layers, so errors can compound in uncontrolled ways. The paper does not discuss this, and 'matching baseline accuracy' is established only empirically on a limited set of tasks. The bias/variance story for the composed model deserves explicit treatment.

Practical savings at typical context lengths are modest. On GSM8K (nk≈341) and MMLU (nk≈417), SANTA needs S=256 to recover baseline accuracy — roughly 60–75% of the sequence length — so value-stage savings are thin outside the long-context regime that motivates the paper. Default SANTA is notably weak (e.g., 5.51% GSM8K accuracy at S=16 vs. 44.63% for S²ANTA-sys), so the usable method is really the stratified/systematic variants.

The Bernoulli qKT contribution (Section 5) is comparatively weak and preliminary: only ~15% key-access reduction on Llama 8B at B=8, meaningful accuracy degradation at B=4 (FWE drops from 94.0 to 70.4 in Table 6), a large ~30–60% L2 score error even with stratification (Appendix C.1), and the most compelling results require BitNet 2B's quantized architecture. It reads as a forward-looking sketch rather than a co-equal contribution, yet it shares billing in the abstract.

The abstract states 'We open-source our kernels at:' followed by no URL, and no anonymous repository link appears anywhere in the manuscript. For a paper whose central empirical contribution is a CUDA kernel, the reproducibility story is incomplete as submitted, despite the otherwise detailed protocols.

The layer-wise REINFORCE budget allocation (Appendix J/K) consumes ~1000 GPU-hours, trains only on DeepSeek 7B, and reports gains (e.g., 66.06 vs. 52.46 on GSM8K) without comparing to simpler allocation heuristics suggested by their own ablation results (Fig. 8), leaving unclear whether RL is necessary for this benefit.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem framing: the paper isolates the memory-bound value-aggregation stage of decode attention and proposes a sampling-based sparsification that is provably unbiased, with a clean variance analysis (Propositions A.2–A.6, Bernstein tail in Appendix B) and a variance-dominance result for stratified sampling.

The systems contribution is real and carefully engineered: the two kernel strategies (S²ANTA-prop with global budget allocation vs. S²ANTA-flash with speculative per-tile sampling and deferred normalization) address a genuine obstacle (the sequential CDF dependency in parallel sampling), and full pseudocode is provided (Appendices O–P).

The evaluation is unusually thorough and honest: bootstrap CIs on all accuracy tables, comparisons to top-k attention (Appendix H), empirical variance measurements matching the 1/S theory (Appendix D), unique-key-count analysis (Table 17), and candid negative results — e.g., admitting that sparse V-access does not materialize in prefill (Table 9) and that S²ANTA-flash requires a 16× larger budget (S=2048 vs. S=128) to match accuracy.

The measurement protocol for the kernel microbenchmark (Appendix Q) is exemplary in its detail: cold-cache thrashing, warmup/timed iteration counts, exact tensor shapes, software versions, and an explicit discussion of the KV-append asymmetry between FlashDecoding and the other backends.

The one-hot ablation (Appendix I) and the REINFORCE-learned per-layer budget allocation (Appendix J) are interesting and independently valuable findings about where attention precision matters across layers.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core idea. Sampling indices from the post-softmax distribution to estimate AV is a straightforward Monte Carlo estimator, and the paper itself cites closely related prior work (Kim & Ko, 2022; MagicPIG's LSH sampling; SparQ). Stratified/systematic sampling is classical survey statistics (Cochran, Lohr). The contribution is largely the combination, the variance-reduction treatment, and the GPU engineering, which is useful but incremental.

The headline speedup is kernel-level only, at batch size 1, on a single consumer GPU (RTX 6000 Ada), for a single model's tensor shapes. The paper acknowledges that end-to-end speedups are subject to Amdahl's Law but never reports an end-to-end decoding speedup, so the practical significance of 1.5× decode-step attention-kernel time at batch size 1 is unclear, particularly for serving workloads with larger batch sizes where the sampling/CDF machinery and multiple-query interactions may behave differently.

There is no latency comparison against other sparse-attention systems at the kernel level (e.g., Quest, SparQ, MagicPIG kernels), so the claimed efficiency advantage over the strongest relevant baselines is only established for exact-attention backends (FlashInfer/FlashDecoding).

The accuracy-matching operating points are selected post hoc from only four RULER tasks at 32k (Table 1) with 500 prompts. That S=128 (≈0.4% of V reads) matches SDPA within CIs is plausible but the CI overlap is a weak equivalence claim; the evaluation does not probe settings where heavy-tailed attention or high-stakes generation would expose accumulated estimator noise across 32 layers and thousands of decoding steps.

The Bernoulli qKᵀ component is substantially less mature: it requires ~30% score error tolerance, is only convincingly demonstrated on BitNet 2B, shows large accuracy collapse at small B on Llama 8B long-context tasks (Table 6, FWE 70.4 vs. 94.0 baseline at B=4), and involves a biased mean-group-query workaround (Eq. 13 requires bias compensation). Including it dilutes the paper's focus without comparable theoretical or systems rigor.

The abstract's open-source statement is incomplete ('We open-source our kernels at:'), which undermines the reproducibility claim at submission time, even though the methodology reporting is otherwise strong.

The systematic-sampling variant S²ANTA-sys — the variant argued to be most hardware-friendly — lacks any variance-reduction guarantee, so the strongest practical claim rests on empirical evidence only (acknowledged, but a gap in the theory-to-systems story).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: sampling S << n_k value rows from the post-softmax distribution yields an unbiased estimator of the value-stage attention output, replacing dense multiply-accumulate with gather-and-add; this is a genuinely different lever than KV retention/eviction methods and is complementary to them.

Solid statistical treatment: unbiasedness of SANTA and S²ANTA variants is proven (Appendix A), stratified sampling has a variance-dominance theorem, and a vector Bernstein concentration bound is provided; empirical variance scaling matches the 1/S theory (Fig. 7).

Real systems contribution: custom CUDA kernels (S²ANTA-prop with exact budget allocation, S²ANTA-flash with speculative per-tile sampling and deferred normalization) with detailed pseudocode (Appendices P–Q), and an unusually careful microbenchmark protocol including an explicit cold-cache/L2-thrashing procedure and honest discussion of what is and is not timed (Appendix R).

Honest treatment of limitations: Appendix F candidly shows SANTA provides no memory-sparse benefit in prefill (~94% of unique V rows read), GQA union-of-queries effects are quantified, sample waste in the flash variant is acknowledged and motivates its 16× larger budget, and the end-to-end gain is explained by an Amdahl-style bandwidth model (1.25×), not oversold.

Extensive empirical evaluation: RULER at 32k and LongBench v2, GSM8K/MMLU, a second model family (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), BitNet 2B, top-k comparisons at matched budgets, one-hot layer ablations, an RL-derived per-layer budget schedule, same-state fidelity analyses, and reproducibility details (prompting/grading tables, licenses, open-sourced kernels).
weaknesses: Modest originality: the unbiasedness of Monte Carlo sampling from the softmax distribution is immediate, and stratified/systematic sampling is textbook material (Cochran); sampling-based attention approximation exists (Kim & Ko, 2022, acknowledged). The novelty is mostly in the systems integration (parallelizable sampling kernels) rather than the estimator itself.

Modest end-to-end significance: even at the best operating points the kernel speedup is ~1.5× and end-to-end decode latency only ~1.25×, confined to long-context, decode-heavy, batch-size-1/6 regimes on a single RTX 6000 Ada; the authors' own Amdahl analysis indicates the benefit shrinks at shorter contexts, larger prefill shares, or lower KV-to-weight bandwidth ratios. No datacenter GPU (A100/H100) results are provided.

Accuracy-matching methodology is somewhat favorable: the reported operating points (S=128 for prop, S=2048 for flash) are the smallest budgets that match SDPA within bootstrap CIs on the selected tasks; S²ANTA-flash needs 16× the budget of prop, substantially eroding its theoretical memory savings (~6.25% of keys read at 32k vs ~1.56% worst case for GQA union).

Bernoulli qK^T is the weakest component: it is only compelling on BitNet 2B (a quantized architecture with unusually robust ternary products); on Llama 8B accuracy drops exceed 2% for B=8 and key-access savings are only ~15–28%, and GQA requires the mean-group-query workaround with additional bias; it reads as an underdeveloped add-on rather than a co-equal contribution.

Stochastic nondeterminism in the decoding path is not deeply addressed: outputs vary run to run, evaluation averages only 3 runs for GSM8K/MMLU and the 32k long-context results use 500 prompts with 3 runs, which may be thin for distinguishing near-baseline accuracies; implications for deployment (reproducible generation, error accumulation over long decode horizons beyond 2048 tokens) are not analyzed.

Compute overhead of the sampling control flow (score stashing, budget allocation kernels, merges) is visible in the kernel results — the S²ANTA variants remain close to FlashInfer rather than far faster despite drastically fewer V reads — suggesting the method's headroom is limited by exactly the machinery needed to make stochastic sampling GPU-friendly.

strengths: The core idea is cleanly motivated and technically correct: SANTA is a provably unbiased estimator of the post-softmax value aggregation (Appendix A), with standard stratified/systematic sampling applied to reduce variance, and the variance-reduction claim for S²ANTA-strat is backed by a proper theorem (A.6).

The systems contribution is real and non-trivial: parallelizing stochastic sampling across tiles requires solving the sequential CDF-dependency problem, and the two proposed kernels (S²ANTA-prop with global budget allocation; S²ANTA-flash with speculative uniform budgets and deferred normalization) are sensible, well-described (Algorithms 2–8), and honestly analyzed, including the 16× sample-budget gap between them (S=128 vs S=2048) attributed to 'sample waste'.

Evaluation is unusually transparent: bootstrap confidence intervals throughout, a microbenchmark appendix (R) with explicit cold-cache protocol, an Amdahl-style bandwidth model that predicts the observed 1.25× end-to-end speedup, same-state fidelity and tile-sensitivity analyses (Appendix U), and unique-key-count measurements (Appendix M) that honestly quantify when the S/n_k memory-savings claim overstates reality (unique keys < S due to sampling with replacement).

Honest scoping: the paper repeatedly clarifies that SANTA is complementary to KV quantization/eviction/selection, that speedups apply to the decode-step kernel and only partially to end-to-end latency, and that prefill benefits are marginal (Appendix F shows >94% unique rows read in prefill).
weaknesses: Limited practical significance relative to the existing sparse-attention landscape. The speedups (1.5× kernel, 1.25× end-to-end) are measured only against exact dense kernels (FlashInfer/FlashDecoding) on a single consumer GPU (RTX 6000 Ada) with a single model (Llama-3.1-8B) and small batch (6). Existing systems that reduce KV access (Quest, MagicPig, SparQ, retrieval-head methods, cited but never benchmarked for speed) already deliver comparable or larger end-to-end gains; a practitioner choosing a decode backend needs those comparisons, which are absent.

Fundamental variance weakness under diffuse attention is acknowledged but not resolved. The estimator's variance is proportional to Σ p_j ||V_j − μ||², so benefits concentrate exactly in the sharply peaked regimes where top-k also works. The paper's own evidence shows this: Table 29 (diffuse multi-hop QA2, 9+ tiles: L2 error 0.19), wide confidence intervals at 32k (e.g., QA2 60.09 ± 4.40), and the need for S=2048 for S²ANTA-flash. Meanwhile top-k is claimed to win on short-context tasks. The unbiasedness advantage over top-k is therefore confined to a regime where the practical gains are smallest.

Stochasticity at decode time is not treated as a first-class limitation. Per-step stochastic attention makes generation non-deterministic at fixed decoding settings, complicates debugging, verification, and reproducible inference deployments, and compounds across steps and layers (the per-layer unbiasedness does not imply the composed output matches the dense model's distribution). The paper reports 3-run averages but never discusses deployment implications of inherent output randomness.

The Bernoulli qK^T contribution underdelivers and is only viable on a heavily quantized model. The estimator induces 30–60% L2 score error (Appendix C.1); on BitNet-2B it works acceptably, but on Llama-8B (Table 8) it needs B=16 to approach baseline and still loses ~6 points on FWE, while only reducing key access to ~72.8%. Presenting this as a co-equal contribution ('Bernoulli qK^T' is a named contribution in the abstract) oversells a fragile, model-specific side result.

The layer-wise RL budget allocation (Appendix K) consumes ~1000 GPU-hours on a 50-GPU Kubernetes cluster to demonstrate what the one-hot ablation already showed qualitatively (early/middle layers need more samples); this is a costly side experiment rather than a deployable technique, and its gains (66.06% vs 52.46% GSM8K at starved budgets) are not translated into an operating point reported anywhere in the main results.

Reproducibility claims are undermined by an incomplete release: the abstract states 'We open-source our kernels at:' with no repository or artifact identifier provided. Given the contribution is primarily kernel engineering, the absence of a verifiable code link at submission is a material weakness.

Theoretical content is thin: unbiasedness and 1/S variance scaling are one-line textbook results, and the Bernstein tail is a direct application of vector concentration inequalities. The novelty over prior Monte Carlo attention approximation (Kim & Ko, 2022) and LSH-based key sampling (MagicPig) is incremental — essentially stratified/systematic variance reduction applied to V-row sampling plus GPU kernel design.

Accuracy matching is partly an artifact of budget selection: operating points are chosen as the smallest S that matches SDPA on the same evaluation suite used to report accuracy (Section 3.4), which invites overfitting of S to the test tasks; generalization of a fixed S to unseen task types at 32k is not demonstrated.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: sampling S << n_k value rows from the post-softmax distribution yields an unbiased estimator of the post-softmax value aggregation, directly targeting the memory-bound decode regime. This is a genuinely different lever from KV eviction/selection methods, and the paper is careful to position it as complementary (Section 6).

The variance-reduction treatment is more principled than typical systems papers: unbiasedness of SANTA and S^2ANTA variants is proven (Appendices A.2, A.4), variance reduction for stratified sampling is proven (Theorem A.6), a vector Bernstein tail is provided (Theorem B.1), and empirical variance scaling is validated (Figure 7, Appendix D).

The GPU engineering is substantive, not cosmetic: the paper identifies the real obstacle (sampling creates a sequential CDF dependency that breaks split-KV parallelism) and develops two concrete kernel strategies (proportional budget allocation with global sync vs. speculative per-tile sampling with deferred normalization), with full pseudocode (Appendices P, Q).

Evaluation covers kernel microbenchmarks, end-to-end batched decoding, and accuracy across GSM8K, MMLU, RULER-style long-context tasks, and LongBench v2, on two models (Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) plus BitNet 2B for the key-side method, with bootstrap confidence intervals and top-k comparisons.

Reproducibility is strong: kernels are open-sourced, measurement protocols are unusually detailed (Appendix R includes cold-cache thrashing, warmup/timed iteration counts, hardware/driver versions), and prompting/grading procedures are documented per benchmark (Appendix O).

Limitations are treated honestly: the paper explicitly states prefill does not benefit (Appendices F, G), that speedups are hardware-dependent, that S^2ANTA-flash requires a 16x larger budget than prop, and that the combined method does not dominate deterministic truncation in all regimes (short-context GSM8K).
weaknesses: The central 'matches baseline accuracy' claim rests on a post-hoc operating-point selection: the smallest S whose accuracy falls within a bootstrap CI of SDPA is chosen per benchmark family. With wide intervals (e.g., QA2 at 32k: 60.2 +/- 4.2) and only ~500 prompts for LongBench v2, this is a weak guarantee of parity; it does not establish that downstream generation quality is preserved across harder or unseen tasks, and per-task tuning of S in deployment would itself be a burden the paper does not address.

Unbiasedness is per-decode-step, but the error accumulates across 32 layers and thousands of generated tokens; the paper measures per-step variance and same-state top-1 agreement, but offers no analysis or experiment on compounding drift over full generations (e.g., distribution of generation lengths, degradation over the 2048-token decode). Table 3's 'avg scored tokens' and GSM8K/MMLU results partially mitigate this, but the multi-step accumulation question is open.

The Bernoulli qK^T contribution is considerably weaker than SANTA: on Llama 8B long-context tasks (Table 8), FWE collapses from 94.0 to 70.7 at B=8 (and 47.3 at B=4), which the text's '<2% accuracy loss' framing obscures by enumerating only the other three tasks. Its strongest results are on BitNet 2B, and the mean-group-query variant (Eq. 6) introduces bias, siting uneasily with the paper's unbiased-estimator narrative. This component feels under-developed relative to its billing as a headline contribution.

Measured speedups are modest and narrow in scope: 1.5x is against the decode-step attention kernel only at batch size 1, on a single GPU (RTX 6000 Ada); end-to-end gains are 1.25-1.29x at batch size 6. No datacenter-GPU (A100/H100) measurements are provided, so the practical significance on the hardware where long-context serving actually runs is extrapolated rather than demonstrated.

The score stage still computes and stashes all attention scores, so K-side traffic is unchanged; the method only halves the effective KV traffic at best (V only), which the 1.5x kernel speedup reflects. Combined with the accuracy-matching budgets (S=128 at 32k, but 2048 for the flash variant, i.e., 16x sample waste), the bandwidth-savings story is less favorable than the abstract's framing suggests.

Sampling with replacement reduces unique keys well below S (Table 20: only 36.4 of 128 unique at S=128), meaning much of the sampled budget is redundant reads; the paper quantifies this but does not resolve it (e.g., without-replacement variants), leaving efficiency on the table.

Nondeterminism is a deployment concern that is not discussed: stochastic attention makes outputs run-to-run variable, complicating reproducibility, debugging, and caching in serving systems; the paper evaluates 3-run averages but never addresses seeding or variance in end-to-end generation quality across runs.
